ops.old: A 2024 study in Health Affairs found that ACOs serving the highest quartile of dual-eligible beneficiaries — patients enrolled in both Medicare and Medicaid, who face the most complex social and clinical needs — were 2.3 times more likely to exit MSSP within three years than ACOs serving lower proportions of dual-eligible patients. The program's financial structure creates systematic pressure against serving the most vulnerable populations.
ops.new: Because MSSP benchmarks and quality scores were built with little adjustment for social risk, ACOs serving high shares of dual-eligible beneficiaries — patients enrolled in both Medicare and Medicaid, who face the most complex social and clinical needs — face weaker financial returns from participation. CMS acknowledged that pressure when it added a health equity adjustment to ACO quality scoring (2023) and a Health Equity Benchmark Adjustment (2025).

ops.sources: CMS fact sheet CY2023 PFS final rule (MSSP health equity adjustment up to 10 quality bonus points); CMS fact sheet CY2025 PFS final rule CMS-1807-F (Health Equity Benchmark Adjustment for ACOs with high LIS/dual shares, from PY2025); no such 2024 Health Affairs study located

ops.old: CMS made its most significant commitment to SDOH risk adjustment in the 2022 MSSP final rule, which introduced a Health Equity Benchmark Adjustment that increases spending benchmarks for ACOs serving high proportions of patients with low-income subsidy status. This acknowledges that high-need populations cost more to manage effectively. However, the 3.5 percent adjustment ceiling is widely considered insufficient by health equity researchers — and it uses low-income subsidy status as an imperfect proxy for the full range of social complexity that drives outcome variation.
ops.new: CMS made its most significant commitment to SDOH risk adjustment in the CY2025 Physician Fee Schedule final rule, which created a Health Equity Benchmark Adjustment — starting in 2025 — that raises spending benchmarks for ACOs serving high proportions of beneficiaries who are dually eligible or receive the Part D low-income subsidy. This acknowledges that high-need populations cost more to manage effectively. Critics note that dual and low-income-subsidy status are imperfect proxies for the full range of social complexity that drives outcome variation.

ops.old: Vermont's All-Payer Model includes an explicit health equity performance requirement — a condition not present in most VBC programs nationally. The AHEAD Model requires participating states to establish measurable health equity goals and report progress annually. Vermont's current equity focus areas include reducing rural-urban disparities in preventive care rates, improving mental health access in rural counties, and addressing the health needs of Vermont's growing refugee and immigrant populations.
ops.new: Vermont's All-Payer Model (2018–2025) set statewide population-health goals — improving access to primary care, reducing deaths from suicide and drug overdose, and reducing the prevalence and morbidity of chronic disease — rather than explicit health equity targets. The AHEAD Model requires participating states to set health equity goals, but Vermont withdrew from AHEAD before its performance period began.
